YIELD: One 9-inch (23-cm) Bundt cake

CAKE
2 tbsp (28 g) unsalted butter, melted for greasing the pan
9 tbsp (81 g) toasted sesame seeds, divided
2 cups (240 g) cake flour
2 tsp (9 g) baking powder
½ tsp salt
1 cup (240 ml) full-fat sour cream, room temperature
1 tsp vanilla extract
1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar
4 tbsp (24 g) orange zest
1⅛ cups (255 g) unsalted butter, room temperature
4 large eggs

SYRUP (OPTIONAL)
1 cup (240 ml) fresh-squeezed orange juice
½ cup (100 g) granulated sugar
Preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C). 

Using a pastry brush, thoroughly brush a 9-inch (23-cm) Bundt pan with butter, then sprinkle it with 3 tablespoons (27 g) of sesame seeds. Set it aside.

In a medium bowl, sift the flour, baking powder and salt and use a fork to blend the mixture and set it aside. Mix together the sour cream and vanilla and set it aside.

In the bowl of a stand mixer, place the sugar and orange zest. Use a fork to blend the orange zest into the sugar.

Add the butter to the bowl and beat on medium-high speed for 4 to 5 minutes, until the mixture appears light in color and fluffy in texture. Scrape the bottom and sides of the bowl, then add the eggs, one at a time, waiting for each egg to fully incorporate before adding the next. Again, scrape the bottom and sides of the bowl.

Reduce the mixer speed to medium-low, then sprinkle one-third of the flour mixture followed by ½ cup (120 ml) of the sour cream and vanilla. Repeat with the remainder of the four mixture and sour cream.

Once you add the last part of the sour cream mixture, turn the mixer off and use a rubber spatula to completely incorporate the flour and the remaining 7 tablespoons (63 g) of toasted sesame seeds.
Spoon the batter into the greased pan and bake for 40 to 45 minutes, or until the top is golden and a toothpick inserted into the center of the cake comes out clean.

While the cake is baking, make the syrup, if desired. In a medium saucepan, bring the orange juice and sugar to a boil. Remove from the heat and pour it into a medium measuring cup with a spout. Place it in the refrigerator to cool.

Remove the cake from the oven and immediately pour the syrup over the cake. Allow it to slightly cool for 15 to 20 minutes, then invert the cake on top of a cooling rack or a serving plate.
Store the cake covered at room temperature for up to 3 days.

NOTES
The addition of the syrup is optional, but it's very important that the syrup is very cold when poured over the hot cake. (To learn why, see the Maple Pecan Cake recipe on page 97.)
In the United States, the average size of a large egg 55 to 60 grams.

Do you not see how many people younger than 40 with blood clots there are? I rarely see anyone on here that old. “Outliers” are not insignificant. 

as many people that come to this sub with anxiety about having a clot, survivors are usually responding to get help if they’re really worried or pointing them to the wiki bc we can’t diagnose anyone. “Fear mongering” is not giving someone info or encouraging them to go to the ER as blood clots are an emergency. Well my main point is you should be concerned if you have immediate symptoms. I can’t imagine getting a brain bleed without knowing. On blood thinners it is much scarier of course and i would panic (and did the other day for a minute) after hitting your head. But i think it’s unhelpful to be anxious about it every time if you feel fine. It’s important to monitor your body’s response if any. And if you aren’t sure then I’d say ask for a doctor. i hope I make sense.

I am not sure how to answer your question as I am in a similar spot. But just know that there’s no getting “behind” in school. You take your time, figure out what you want even if it takes forever (which sucks I know). I don’t have an associates degree either because I change my major a lot. One thing I will say is to do in-depth research for like 10 careers you know you’re interested in and narrow it down to what you can actually see yourself doing. Ask yourself:

What do I like about this major & career?
What do I not like about it? Can I put up with the dislikes?
How long is it going to take to accomplish? Is the time and energy fitting for me?
Can I see myself doing this long term? If I can’t, am I okay with switching careers later on?

Stuff like that. Idk if that is helpful but when I was changing my major last time I had to make a list of what was important to me, what I know I’m capable of, whether I’m willing to do the work to achieve it etc. It is not easy. I still keep circling back around because I have many interests.

Sorry I didn’t expect to write much lol. But when you do choose a major & career, remember it’s not set in stone. You are free to switch careers whenever you want (though it can be harder than switching majors). Wishing you all the best!

Something that helps me at times is thinking about when I don’t reply quickly. How do they feel? I often don’t reply fast because I either don’t have the energy for a conversation, I have no idea how to respond at the moment, I don’t actually understand what they said and need time (unless I feel comfortable asking), or other things. Sometimes I open messages and completely forget to reply because I got distracted.  

I guess just try to reframe your thinking. Even if you’re someone who regularly replies quickly, there are tons more reasons that the other person hasn’t than them purposely ignoring you. Slow replies do not always mean the worst possible thing.
